public_rationale: The plain claim is that OpenAI was losing money in 2025 and needed outside investors to keep going. Microsoft's filing implies OpenAI lost about $11.5 billion in July–September 2025. OpenAI's investor documents, as reported, projected a 2025 net loss of about $9 billion. Even the FT's friendliest estimate, excluding one-time charges, puts the 2025 loss near $8 billion. Fortune reported that the strategy 'requires near-constant fundraising to keep the startup alive.' OpenAI's CFO said the company could break even if it chose to, but that is a claim, not a result. 'At the mercy of investors' is rhetoric. The verifiable core, losses plus dependence on outside capital, holds.
limitations: Quarterly loss is a press calculation from Microsoft's equity-method share, not an OpenAI disclosure.
Annual figures come from leaked or reported documents, not a public OpenAI filing.
Whether reliance on investors amounts to being 'at their mercy' is a judgment; OpenAI raised money easily in 2026.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Because OpenAI is losing money and can't stand on its own for long, it is at the mercy of investors.

statement.excerpt: Since they are losing money and can’t stand on their own two feet for long. That puts them at the mercy of investors.

from_speaker: can't stand on their own two feet for long
That puts them at the mercy of investors
our_interpretation: He names no period, so I read 'are losing money' as describing calendar 2025, the year in progress when he posted on 2025-12-03 and the latest period with public loss data.
Plain reading: OpenAI was running large net losses and could not pay for its operations and planned spending from its own revenue, so it needed repeated outside funding to keep going.
'At the mercy of investors' is rhetoric. I score it as reliance on outside capital, not as proof that investors imposed harsh terms.
criteria.support_condition: Credible reports show OpenAI ran net losses in 2025 and needed ongoing outside fundraising to fund operations and spending.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible reports show OpenAI was profitable or cash-flow positive in 2025, or could fund itself without new outside capital.

evidence.excerpt: Microsoft’s admission that it shaved $3.1 billion off its net income to account for its share of OpenAI losses therefore suggests OpenAI lost about $11.5 billion during the quarter.
evidence.explanation: Microsoft's filing shows a large share of OpenAI losses for July–September 2025, implying an OpenAI loss of about $11.5 billion that quarter.

evidence.excerpt: The company anticipates total spending of roughly $22 billion this year against $13 billion in sales, resulting in a net loss of $9 billion
evidence.publisher: Fortune (citing documents obtained by The Wall Street Journal)
evidence.explanation: OpenAI's own investor documents, as reported, projected a 2025 net loss of about $9 billion.

evidence.excerpt: Altman’s strategy for OpenAI requires near-constant fundraising to keep the startup alive
evidence.explanation: Supports the dependence half of the claim: the business needed continual outside funding to keep going.

evidence.excerpt: OpenAI’s losses for 2025 were closer to $8 billion once you strip out all of the stuff that should be one-time costs.
evidence.explanation: Even on the friendliest reading, without one-time conversion charges, OpenAI lost about $8 billion in 2025. The headline audited loss was $38.5 billion.

evidence.excerpt: OpenAI Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar said last week the company has healthy margins and could break even if it wanted to.
evidence.explanation: The company's counterpoint: it says its losses are a choice to invest, not a sign it cannot stand alone. This is a claim, not a result.
